desc:
There are n sealed bags of cookies; bags[i] is the number of cookies in bag i. Bags cannot be opened or split. They are handed out to k children, each bag going to exactly one child (a child may end up with no bag at all).

The unfairness of a distribution is the largest number of cookies that any single child receives. Return the smallest unfairness that can be achieved.

For example, bags = [8, 15, 10, 20, 8] and k = 2 gives 31 (one child takes 8 + 15 + 8 = 31, the other 10 + 20 = 30).
hints: Every bag has k possible owners, so there are k<sup>n</sup> distributions. Think about how to explore them while discarding hopeless ones early.
Process the bags one by one, keeping the current total of every child. If the largest total already reaches the best answer found so far, stop exploring that branch.

Two symmetries cut a lot of work: handle bags from largest to smallest, and never try giving a bag to two children who currently have the same total (the results are mirror images). Also stop immediately when the best answer equals the trivial lower bound max(max bag, ceil(sum / k)).
editorial: This is a min-max partition problem, which is NP-hard in general, so with n ≤ 12 we use a pruned backtracking search. Keep an array loads of the k children's totals. For bag i (sorted in decreasing order), try handing it to each child, update the load, recurse, and undo.

Pruning makes it fast. (1) Prune when the largest load reaches the current best answer: this branch cannot improve it. (2) Starting with an upper bound from a greedy assignment (give each bag to the currently lightest child) gives strong pruning from the start. (3) Skip a child whose load equals the load of a child already tried for this bag. In particular all empty children are equivalent, so only one of them is tried. (4) Stop all search when the best equals the lower bound max(max(bags), ceil(sum(bags) / k)).
Large bags first is important: placing big items early makes the loads differ quickly and lets pruning fire close to the root.
time: O(k<sup>n</sup>) worst case, much less with pruning
solution:
def minLargestShare(bags, k):
    bags = sorted(bags, reverse=True)
    n = len(bags)
    lower = max(bags[0], -(-sum(bags) // k))
    loads = [0] * k
    for b in bags:
        loads[loads.index(min(loads))] += b
    best = max(loads)
    loads = [0] * k

    def go(i, cur):
        nonlocal best
        if best <= lower or cur >= best:
            return
        if i == n:
            best = cur
            return
        seen = set()
        for c in range(k):
            if loads[c] in seen:
                continue
            seen.add(loads[c])
            loads[c] += bags[i]
            go(i + 1, max(cur, loads[c]))
            loads[c] -= bags[i]

    go(0, 0)
    return best
